Note🌱 SPROuT



SPROuT – Science Powered through Reproducibility, Openness, and Teamwork 
📍 Location: Seminarium, Department of Botany
🎓 Credits: 3 ECTS
💻 Format: Practical, group-based sessions in RStudio (bring your own laptop)
🎯 Course Code: 

Description
SPROuT is a five-day, hands-on workshop focused on mastering the principles of reproducibility, openness, and teamwork in scientific research.
Designed for master’s and PhD students, the course offers a practical and engaging approach to building modern research workflows using R, Git/GitHub, and Quarto.
Participants will learn how to organise their projects efficiently, write clean and reproducible code, manage their work with version control, collaborate effectively within research teams, and publish transparent, reproducible results. Through interactive group-based sessions in RStudio, students will gain the confidence to apply Open Science practices in their own research—making their work more robust, collaborative, and shareable.


Daily Themes

Organise – Set up your project structure, manage your environment, and learn the principles of Open Science.

Analyse – Write readable, reproducible, scalable R code with good coding etiquette.

Save – Implement version control with Git/GitHub to track, protect, and manage your research.

Collaborate – Learn to work in teams using GitHub for transparent project collaboration.

Publish – Communicate and share your research openly.



Expected Learning Outcomes

Understand the principles of Open Science 🌐 and reproducibility ♻️.

Apply best practices for data and project organisation 🗂️.

Use Git/GitHub for version control 📚.

Manage projects and collaborate using GitHub 🧑‍💼.

Create reproducible reports using Quarto 📜.

Share research openly following FAIR principles and modern publishing standards 🔓.

Note📊 Biostatistics for biologists



Statistics in biology and design of ecological experiments
🎓 Credits: 5 ECTS
🎯 SIS Course Code: 

Expected Learning Outcomes

Distinguish among variable types and select appropriate numerical summaries and graphical displays 📊.
Translate a biological or ecological question into a model by identifying the response and predictor variables 🧩.
Use the linear model as a fundamental analytical tool 📈.
Interpret linear-model parameters (\(a\), \(b\)) and assess the strength of a relationship (\(R^2\)) 🔎.
Interpret effect estimates and uncertainty, including confidence intervals 🎯.
Interpret p-values in context 🧪.
Assess model assumptions and determine whether they are satisfied ✅.
Work with multiple predictors and explain the consequences of correlated predictors 🧮.
Recognise and interpret interactions between predictors 🔀.
Compare candidate models using AIC and justify the choice of a final model ⚖️.
Recognise nonlinearity and select a simple solution, such as a transformation or an appropriate functional form 📉.
Recognise hierarchical data structures, including repeated measurements, sites, and blocks, and determine when the model needs to be extended 🧱.
Select an appropriate model for categorical responses and explain why a linear model (lm) is unsuitable for binary data (0/1) 🔢.
Construct a complete analytical workflow in R: data import → visualisation → modelling → diagnostics → interpretation ♻️.

title: Planetary Boundaries Working Group
text:
website
  

  
  
Planetary Boundaries and Safe Operating Spaces is a working group within Past Global Changes - PAGES, aiming to link palaeoecology with planetary boundaries to define variability and changes over decades to millennia.



To guide us towards sustainable futures, this working group explores how past ecological data can help define safe operating spaces for critical Earth system processes. By studying long-term data on land use, biosphere integrity, freshwater, and biochemical flows, we aim to model changes and identify potential tipping points.
This approach provides insights into stabilising Earth system processes by aiming for “Holocene-like” conditions, essential in mitigating ongoing environmental crises.
For more information, visit the project website.



As a committee member, I contribute expertise in palaeoecology and long-term data analysis, helping to develop and coordinate the project.

Molecular Ecology of Medieval European Landscapes (MEMELAND) is an ERC Synergy project running from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2031.


MEMELAND will develop a species-level ecological history of Europe from the Roman era to the present. The project combines sedimentary ancient DNA, lipid biomarkers, archaeobotanical evidence, pollen, and climate records to investigate how medieval land use, technology, and social organisation left persistent effects on European landscapes and biodiversity.
The project studies paired lakes across northern and central Europe to compare landscapes associated with high-status medieval sites against nearby areas with less archaeological influence. This long-term perspective will support biodiversity conservation, sustainable land management, and heritage-informed restoration under climate change.
For project news and further information, visit the MEMELAND website. The European Commission CORDIS record provides the authoritative grant details.

Humans on Planet Earth - Long-term impacts on biosphere dynamics (HOPE) is a 5.5-year European Research Council Advanced Grant project running from 1 January 2018 to the end of 2023. It addresses a critical question in Earth system science - what was the impact of prehistoric people on the biosphere and its dynamics?



To test the recently proposed hypothesis that prehistoric human impact about 6000 years ago altered the fundamental ecological processes which determine the assembly, ecological structure, and dynamics of terrestrial plant communities. Proponents of this hypothesis argue that the use of past ‘natural experiments’ and of the past as an analogue to the uncertain future of Earth in the ‘Anthropocene’ is a ‘flawed strategy’ and uniformitarianism should be discarded. As much of Earth system science relies on such ‘natural experiments’ and depends on the concept of uniformitarianism, it is clearly imperative to test critically and robustly this hypothesis and related arguments and far-reaching conclusions.
To test the associated hypothesis that the inter-relationships (correlations) between estimates of ecosystem properties such as turnover, taxonomic and functional diversity, and co-occurrence patterns changed during the Holocene in response to prehistoric human activities.

Check out the project website for more information.

title: Functional Vegetation Paleoecology
text: Functional Vegetation Paleoecology is a 4-year research project funded by PRIMUS, starting on 1st June 2025.

title: Functional Vegetation Paleoecology
text:
Project Description
Anticipating ecosystem changes under global climate change presents a complex challenge that demands interdisciplinary solutions. By leveraging paleoecological vegetation data and functional ecology methods, the project aims to estimate spatio-temporal variations of functional ecosystem properties beyond the point of human observation, thereby gaining an unprecedented understanding of global vegetation patterns.
Through the integration of global fossil pollen data with modern plant traits, the project aims to identify regions most vulnerable to climate change based on paleoecological insights. Utilizing probabilistic Bayesian models, the project will address taxonomic uncertainties and estimate variations in functional ecosystem properties globally, spanning since the Last Glacial Maximum.

title: Functional Vegetation Paleoecology
text:
Project Goals

Aim 1: Integrate global fossil pollen data with modern plant traits to account for uncertainties.
Aim 2: Estimate global functional ecosystem properties since the Last Glacial Maximum.
Aim 3: Assess current ecosystems’ Safe Operating Space to help mitigate the impact of climate change (see my participation Planetary Boundaries project).

title: BIODYNAMICS
text:
Project description
The BIODYNAMICS project aims to address the need for predicting biodiversity and ecosystem alteration under global climate change. Life scientists need to be able to predict biodiversity and ecosystem alteration under global climate change. However, scenarios able to predict biodiversity trajectories are wishful thinking as biotic interactions in novel environments or among newly coexisting species are not sufficiently understood. By investigating local processes of species interactions, BIODYNAMICS will contribute crucial insights into how these interactions shape continental and global biodiversity patterns over the past 20 thousand years (ka). BIODYNAMICS will develop innovative approaches that allow estimating ecosystem functioning, especially the essential biotic interactions, at 3 major ecological scales (spatial, temporal, and taxonomic), spanning from individual plants in local sites to whole continents and from 20 ka to the present.
It will do so using a newly compiled publicly available multidisciplinary database that integrates present and past global vegetation records with their functional traits and climate data. This database will serve as a valuable resource for advancing knowledge in eco-informatics, community ecology, climatology, and paleo- and neo-ecology.
A key aspect of BIODYNAMICS is to utilize insights from the past to inform future predictions of global biodiversity patterns, which are anticipated to be influenced by anthropogenic climate change. By fostering interdisciplinary cooperation between these scientific disciplines, the project aims to enhance our understanding and quantification of biotic interactions in both historical and contemporary contexts. These insights will be instrumental in predicting ecological responses to global change, thereby ensuring the preservation of ecosystem services that are essential for our society.

title: BIODYNAMICS
text:
Project goals
Improve the capacity to predict global biodiversity patterns using a new multidisciplinary framework to infer biotic interactions of vegetation, and identify how local-scale biotic interactions scaled up to maintain biodiversity patterns at various spatial scales during the last 20 ka.

title: Snippets and tasks
text: Snippets and tasks travel with the VS Code profile through Settings Sync. The scripts that the tasks run do not: they live in ~/.vscode-scripts/ and have to be copied to each machine by hand (see Profiles and Settings Sync).

title: Snippets and tasks
Snippets and tasks
R versions
text:
Nothing in my synced settings names an R version or a path:

r.consolePath is "radian", found on PATH.
r.executablePath is not set, so vscode-R uses R.exe on PATH, which is rig’s shortcut in C:\Program Files\R\bin.
The R Debugger extension reads only the old r.rpath.windows. That is not set either, so it also uses R.exe on PATH. vscode-R shows a one-time warning about this whenever R Debugger is installed; without a project pin there is nothing to do.
radian also starts the R on PATH, unless R_HOME is set or --r-binary is given.

So the R version is whatever rig default says on that machine. The settings stay identical everywhere, which is what lets Settings Sync carry them.

title: R versions
section: Switch R for the whole machine
text:
Switch R for the whole machine
rig list              # installed versions; * marks the default
rig add release       # install the newest release (or: rig add 4.5)
rig default 4.6.2     # use it everywhere
Then open a new R terminal. No VS Code change is needed. Remember that a new R version starts with an empty package library: install the R packages for it.

title: R versions
section: Pin one project to a version
text:
Pin one project to a version
Sometimes a project needs an older R, for example one whose renv.lock was made with R 4.5.1. The pin goes into that project’s workspace settings, .vscode/settings.json, which override the profile.

With the R Version Switcher extension
I wrote (well, vibe-coded) a small extension for this: R Version Switcher. It works with rig and the R extension. It is not on the Marketplace; install the .vsix from its latest release with code --install-extension r-version-switcher-1.2.0.vsix --profile R. Its commands:







Command
What it does




R: Switch Version
Pick an installed R version for this workspace. The list marks the current one, the system default and the one in renv.lock.


R: Use R Version from renv.lock
Switch to the version recorded in renv.lock; offers to install it (or the newest patch of the same minor version) if it is missing.


R: Show Current Version
The workspace’s R version and path, and whether the path is valid.


R: Add Version / R: Remove Version
rig add / rig rm, run as a VS Code task so you see the output.


R: Set System Default Version
rig default, without touching the workspace.


R: Install Rtools
Installs the Rtools versions your R versions need but do not have.



A status bar item shows the workspace’s R version and turns yellow when it differs from renv.lock. Click it to switch. That pairs well with the project template, which uses renv.
The extension writes the same settings as the manual method below, using rig’s version link when it exists, including r.rpath.windows when R Debugger is installed. Restart the R terminal after switching. It does not set QUARTO_R (version 1.2.0), so quarto render needs the separate step for Quarto.


By hand
First, once per machine, create the version-named shortcuts:
rig system make-links   # creates R-4.6.2.exe, R-4.5.1.exe, ... in C:\Program Files\R\bin
Then in the project’s .vscode/settings.json:
{
  "r.executablePath": "R-4.5.1.exe",
  "r.consoleArgs": ["--no-save", "--no-restore", "--r-binary=R-4.5.1.exe"],
  "r.rpath.windows": "R-4.5.1.exe"
}

r.executablePath is the R that vscode-R uses for the language server, help and the workspace viewer.
r.consoleArgs is passed to radian. --r-binary makes radian start that R. The first two arguments are vscode-R’s default, which the workspace value would otherwise replace.
r.rpath.windows is for the R Debugger extension, which reads only this older setting. Without it, the debugger runs the default R instead of the pinned one. vscode-R marks the setting as deprecated, but asks to keep it, with the same value as r.executablePath, while R Debugger is installed. Leave it out if you do not use R Debugger.
R-4.5.1.exe is found on PATH, so the file contains no user name and no install path. It works on every machine that has R 4.5.1 through rig, so the file can be committed.
Keep the .exe. vscode-R adds .exe only to names without an extension, and R-4.5.1 looks like it has one (.1), so without it vscode-R does not find R. radian accepts both.
A full path such as C:\\Program Files\\R\\R-4.5.1\\bin\\R.exe also works and contains no user name, but it is Windows-only.

To check which R a terminal really runs: R.version.string in the console, or radian --r-binary=R-4.5.1 --version in PowerShell.


Quarto projects
The .vscode/settings.json pin reaches only vscode-R and radian. quarto render does not read it: it uses the Rscript on PATH, which is rig’s default. In a project with renv that shows up as missing packages, because renv keeps a separate project library for each R version (renv/library/windows/R-4.x/...), and the default R looks in the wrong one (symptom).
To pin Quarto as well, set QUARTO_R in a file called _environment.local at the root of the Quarto project:
QUARTO_R="C:/Program Files/R/R-4.5.1/bin"
and keep the file out of git, because the path is machine-specific. In .gitignore:
_environment.local

The value is the R install’s bin folder, not rig’s R-4.5.1.exe shortcut. Quarto looks for Rscript.exe in the folder it is given, and next to the shortcut, in C:\Program Files\R\bin, that is rig’s default again. (I have not tried the shortcut; I expect it to fail for that reason.)
QUARTO_R set in the shell, or in a committed _environment, works too, but _environment.local keeps the path out of the repository.
Lines starting with # are comments, so the file can say why it is there.

title: Outside VS Code
text: Settings Sync only carries what is inside VS Code (what it does not carry). The rest lives in a few small files. I keep them in the OneDrive Documents folder, so OneDrive shares them between my machines. Because they are shared, they follow the same rule as the VS Code settings. So they contain no user names, and anything only one machine has (a D: drive, TinyTeX) is checked before use.

title: Outside VS Code
text:
.Rprofile
R runs a user .Rprofile at start-up. It reads:

a .Rprofile in the current folder, if there is one;
otherwise, the one in R_USER, which on Windows is the Documents folder (with OneDrive folder backup, that is OneDrive\Documents).

In renv projects, the project’s own .Rprofile activates renv, and renv does not load the user .Rprofile unless you set renv.config.user.profile = TRUE. So none of the below applies inside renv projects (which includes projects from my project template).
A stray .Rprofile in a project or home folder silently replaces the user one; keep one. Check which one wins with Sys.getenv("R_USER") and file.exists(".Rprofile").

What it does, block by block








Block
What it does
Why




httpgd in VS Code
Only when interactive and inside VS Code (TERM_PROGRAM == "vscode") and if httpgd is installed: sets vsc.rstudioapi, vsc.use_httpgd, vsc.plot = FALSE, and makes httpgd the default graphics device.
Plots go to the httpgd viewer in VS Code. vsc.rstudioapi lets packages that call rstudioapi (add-ins, usethis) work in VS Code.


btw
Starts btw::btw_mcp_session() when interactive, only if btw is installed for this R version.
Lets coding assistants (through MCP) see the live R session: objects, help, installed packages.


radian options
radian.auto_match = FALSE, radian.auto_indentation = FALSE.
radian would otherwise insert closing brackets and indent as you type.


RStudio’s pandoc
Sets RSTUDIO_PANDOC to RStudio’s bundled pandoc folder, if it exists.
rmarkdown outside RStudio then finds pandoc without a separate install.


Temporary folder
Sets TEMP/TMP to D:/Temp, only if that folder exists.
Big temporary files go to a second drive on the machine that has one. On other machines nothing changes.


TinyTeX
Appends TinyTeX’s bin\windows to PATH, if installed and not there yet.
PDF output from R Markdown / Quarto started from R.



The quarto R package and rmarkdown find Quarto on PATH, which is the all-users install.


Show the full file: .Rprofile

# User .Rprofile. R reads it from R_USER (= OneDrive\Documents), so OneDrive
# shares it between machines: keep it machine-neutral (no user names, no
# paths that exist on only one machine; guard anything optional).

# VS Code: plots go to httpgd (vscode-R shows them in its viewer).
if (interactive() && Sys.getenv("TERM_PROGRAM") == "vscode") {
  if ("httpgd" %in% .packages(all.available = TRUE)) {
    options(vsc.rstudioapi = TRUE)
    options(vsc.use_httpgd = TRUE)
    options(vsc.plot = FALSE)
    options(device = function(...) {
      httpgd::hgd(silent = FALSE)
    })
  }
}

# Expose the session to coding assistants (MCP), when btw is installed for
# this R version (each R version has its own library).
if (interactive() && requireNamespace("btw", quietly = TRUE)) {
  btw::btw_mcp_session()
}

# radian: no automatic bracket matching or indentation.
options(radian.auto_match = FALSE)
options(radian.auto_indentation = FALSE)

local({
  # Pandoc bundled with RStudio, for rmarkdown outside RStudio.
  rstudio_pandoc <- "C:/Program Files/RStudio/resources/app/bin/quarto/bin/tools"
  if (dir.exists(rstudio_pandoc)) {
    Sys.setenv(RSTUDIO_PANDOC = rstudio_pandoc)
  }

  # Large temporary files on a second drive, where the machine has one.
  temp_dir <- "D:/Temp"
  if (dir.exists(temp_dir)) {
    Sys.setenv(TEMP = temp_dir, TMP = temp_dir)
  }

  # TinyTeX (LaTeX for PDF output), if installed and not already on PATH.
  tinytex_bin <- file.path(Sys.getenv("APPDATA"), "TinyTeX", "bin", "windows")
  path_entries <- normalizePath(
    strsplit(Sys.getenv("PATH"), ";", fixed = TRUE)[[1]],
    winslash = "/",
    mustWork = FALSE
  )
  if (
    dir.exists(tinytex_bin) &&
      !normalizePath(tinytex_bin, winslash = "/") %in% path_entries
  ) {
    Sys.setenv(PATH = paste(Sys.getenv("PATH"), tinytex_bin, sep = ";"))
  }
})

Download Rprofile.R
(Published as Rprofile.R so that browsers show it; save it as .Rprofile in your Documents folder.)

title: Outside VS Code
text:
PATH rules
Most of my R-in-VS-Code problems have come from PATH. The rules:







Rule
Why




C:\Program Files\R\bin (rig’s shortcuts) is on PATH.
R, Rscript and radian then use rig’s default version.


No version folder such as C:\Program Files\R\R-x.y.z\bin on PATH.
It pins one R version and overrides rig.


No R_HOME environment variable (check both user and system).
Same: radian and R use it before anything else.


Python312\ and Python312\Scripts\ come before any other Python.
python and radian must be the 3.12 ones.


C:\Program Files\Quarto\bin is the only Quarto on PATH.
R, VS Code and the terminal then use the same Quarto.


After any change: quit and restart VS Code.
VS Code and its terminals keep the PATH they started with.



To check what a new process will see, without restarting anything:
$env:Path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "Machine") + ";" +
            [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User")
Get-Command R.exe, python, radian, quarto | Select-Object Name, Source
[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("R_HOME", "User")
[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("R_HOME", "Machine")
radian --version

title: Outside VS Code
text:
Package libraries
Each R version (major.minor) has its own user library, %LOCALAPPDATA%\R\win-library\<x.y>. R 4.5.x versions share win-library\4.5; a new minor version starts with an empty library. That is why the R packages are installed once per R version.

text:
Everything can be done from PowerShell with winget, which comes with Windows 11.
Install R before Rtools and the R packages, and Python before radian. After changing PATH, programs only see the change when they are started again (see step 10).

title: Install, in order
text:
1. VS Code
winget install Microsoft.VisualStudioCode
Or download it from https://code.visualstudio.com/Download (the User Installer is fine). Then turn on Settings Sync (the account icon, bottom left) and sign in. On a machine that already has a synced set-up, this brings back the profiles, settings, keybindings, snippets, tasks and extensions. Read Profiles and Settings Sync first: two R settings do not sync unless you tell VS Code to sync them.

title: Install, in order
text:
2. rig, then R
rig installs and switches R versions. It keeps the set-up free of machine-specific paths: VS Code and radian use “the R on PATH”, and rig decides which version that is.
winget install Posit.rig
Open a new terminal (so it sees rig on PATH), then:
rig add release          # the current R release; accept the UAC prompt
rig default 4.6.2        # the version used everywhere; `rig list` shows what is installed
rig system make-links    # version-named shortcuts: R-4.6.2, R-4.5.1, ...
rig system fix-r-alias   # make `R` start R in PowerShell

rig add release looks stuck with no output when it is waiting for the UAC prompt, which can be hidden behind other windows.
rig add 4.5.1 (or rig add 4.5) installs an older version next to it.
In PowerShell, R is a built-in alias for Invoke-History. rig system fix-r-alias removes that alias in your PowerShell profile (see Outside VS Code).
rig puts its shortcuts (R.exe, Rscript.exe, R-4.6.2.exe, …) in C:\Program Files\R\bin, which must be on PATH. Do not also add a version folder such as C:\Program Files\R\R-x.y.z\bin to PATH, and do not set R_HOME: both pin one version and override rig (see Troubleshooting).
rig does not install Rtools (step 6).

title: Install, in order
text:
3. RStudio (optional)
winget install Posit.RStudio
rig registers its R versions with RStudio, so there is nothing else to set up. Its bundled pandoc is also used by my .Rprofile (Outside VS Code).

title: Install, in order
text:
4. Python (python.org build)
radian is a Python program, so it needs Python. I use Python 3.12, the python.org build, not the Microsoft Store one:
winget install Python.Python.3.12 --override "/quiet InstallAllUsers=0 PrependPath=1 Include_launcher=1 Include_test=0"

PrependPath=1 puts Python312\ and Python312\Scripts\ on your user PATH. Scripts\ is where radian.exe will be.
If another Python is installed (a Store one, or 3.13+), 3.12 must come first on PATH. Check in a new terminal: python --version and Get-Command radian must both point to Python312.

title: Install, in order
text:
5. radian
radian is a better R console: syntax highlighting, multi-line editing, and autocompletion.
python -m pip install -U radian
radian --version   # shows the radian, R and Python versions it uses
radian --version should report the R version you set with rig default. If it shows another one, see Troubleshooting.
If the install fails while compiling, install the Microsoft C++ Build Tools.

title: Install, in order
text:
6. Rtools
Rtools compiles R packages from source (needed for GitHub packages such as vscDebugger, and for your own packages).
winget install RProject.Rtools

Rtools 4.5 covers R 4.5.0 and later, including 4.6.x. There is no separate Rtools 4.6.
Check in R: pkgbuild::has_build_tools() should be TRUE, and Sys.which("make") should point into C:\rtools45\.

title: Install, in order
text:
7. The R packages
These are needed once per R version: each R version has its own package library, and a new version starts empty.
install.packages(c("languageserver", "remotes", "httpgd", "devtools", "lintr", "styler", "btw"))
remotes::install_github("ManuelHentschel/vscDebugger")



Package
Why

Autocompletion, go to definition, hover help and diagnostics in VS Code.


vscDebugger
The R debugger behind the R Debugger extension. Only on GitHub, so it needs Rtools.


httpgd
The plot viewer. VS Code shows plots from it (r.plot.backend: "httpgd").


devtools
Package development; brings usethis (used by the scratch project task).


lintr
Linting in the editor. Needs lintr 3.3.0-1 or newer.

Formatting, used by languageserver for “Format Document”.


btw
Exposes the R session to coding assistants (MCP). My .Rprofile starts it when installed. Optional.

title: Install, in order
text:
8. Quarto
winget install Posit.Quarto
This installs Quarto for all users in C:\Program Files\Quarto.

title: Install, in order
text:
10. Restart VS Code and test
Quit every VS Code window and start it again. VS Code and all its terminals keep the PATH they were started with, and Developer: Reload Window does not refresh it.
Then:

Open an R file, then Command Palette → Terminal: Create New Terminal. With the settings in place, it opens radian (the default terminal profile is “R Terminal”).
Approve the sess installation. The first R terminal for each R version shows a pop-up asking to install sess, a small helper package of vscode-R that connects the console to VS Code: the workspace view, help, plots, and R: attached in the status bar. It goes into vscode-R’s own library, not your package library, and vscode-R asks again when it updates its copy. Approve it and wait for the R prompt; do not reload the window while the pop-up is open (why).
Run plot(1:10). The plot opens in the httpgd viewer beside the editor.
Run R.version.string. It shows rig’s default version.

If something fails, see Troubleshooting.

Overlaps and clean-up candidates
Extensions that do the same job twice, or that seem to be left over. These are candidates to check, not decisions.

Icon themes. vscode-icons-team.vscode-icons is the active theme in R (and Default), pkief.material-icon-theme in R-Lecturer (workbench.iconTheme). R has both installed but uses one. pkief.material-product-icons in R-Lecturer is installed but not selected.
Docker. docker.docker, ms-azuretools.vscode-docker and ms-azuretools.vscode-containers are all in R. Container Tools has taken over the Docker extension, which now depends on it. Docker DX adds Dockerfile and Compose editing on top. Dev Containers works without any of them, as long as Docker itself is installed.
CSV. mechatroner.rainbow-csv, repreng.csv and phplasma.csv-to-table in R; mechatroner.rainbow-csv and grapecity.gc-excelviewer (which also opens CSV) in R-Lecturer.
SQLite. alexcvzz.vscode-sqlite, qwtel.sqlite-viewer and, in R-Lecturer, mtxr.sqltools-driver-sqlite all open SQLite databases.
TODO comments. gruntfuggly.todo-tree and wayou.vscode-todo-highlight. Todo Tree highlights the tags as well.
DBML. matt-meyers.vscode-dbml is marked deprecated by its author. nicolas-liger.dbml-viewer is the other DBML extension.
AI assistants. R has github.copilot-chat, anthropic.claude-code, openai.chatgpt (with openai.codex-audio), continue.continue and coderabbit.coderabbit-vscode. They do not conflict, but each adds a view, a sign-in and background work.
R Markdown. tianyishi.rmarkdown sits next to reditorsupport.r, which already handles .Rmd files (chunks, knitting), and quarto.quarto, which renders them too. It may still matter for bookdown or blogdown projects.
R formatters. posit.air-vscode and reditorsupport.r (through the styler package) both format R code. R uses REditorSupport.r as editor.defaultFormatter.
SCSS formatters. michelemelluso.code-beautifier and sibiraj-s.vscode-scss-formatter both format SCSS in R-Lecturer; [scss] picks the second.
Spelling and grammar. streetsidesoftware.code-spell-checker in both, znck.grammarly in R, valentjn.vscode-ltex in R-Lecturer. R-Lecturer also has a Grammarly setting without the extension.
LaTeX. james-yu.latex-workshop and mathematic.vscode-latex both provide LaTeX language support.
Markdown preview. shd101wyy.markdown-preview-enhanced duplicates much of the built-in preview with bierner.markdown-mermaid.
Not used for R work. zrachod.mono-snippets, sumneko.lua (unless you write Quarto filters) and ms-mssql.sql-bindings-vscode (comes with ms-mssql.mssql).

title: Extensions
text:
Installing them

With Settings Sync
With Settings Sync on, VS Code installs each profile’s extensions when it downloads the profile on a new machine (see Profiles and Settings Sync).


Not on the Marketplace
Settings Sync and install_extensions.ps1 install extensions from the Marketplace, so neither can install the R Version Switcher. On each machine, download the .vsix from its latest release and run:
code --install-extension r-version-switcher-1.2.0.vsix --profile R


Manual rebuild
install_extensions.ps1 reads a list with one extension id per line and installs it into a named profile:

It checks that code (the VS Code command-line tool) is on PATH.
It skips blank lines, lines starting with #, and extensions the profile already has (code --list-extensions --profile <name>).
It installs the rest with code --install-extension <id> --profile <name>.
At the end it lists the failures and exits with code 1 if there were any.

The VS Code command line only installs into a profile that already exists; for a missing one it reports Profile '<name>' not found. The script then opens VS Code once with code --profile <name>, which creates an empty profile, waits until the profile is there, and continues. If that does not work, create the profile in the Profiles editor (File → Preferences → Profiles) and run the script again. Use -Profile Default for the Default profile.
Put the script and the lists in one folder, then run, for example:
pwsh -File install_extensions.ps1 -Profile R -List extensions-R.txt
pwsh -File install_extensions.ps1 -Profile R-Lecturer
Without -List, the script uses extensions-<Profile>.txt next to itself. It needs PowerShell 7 (pwsh).


Show the full file: install_extensions.ps1

#Requires -Version 7.0
<#
.SYNOPSIS
    Install the VS Code extensions from a list file into a VS Code profile.

.DESCRIPTION
    Reads a text file with one extension id per line (as written by
    `code --list-extensions`), and installs every id that the profile does not
    have yet. Blank lines and lines starting with "#" are ignored. Failures are
    listed at the end and the script then exits with code 1.

    The VS Code CLI installs extensions only into a profile that already
    exists: `code --profile <name> --install-extension <id>` stops with
    "Profile '<name>' not found." The only CLI way to create a profile is to
    open a window with it (`code --profile <name>`), which creates an empty
    one. So when the profile is missing, the script does that once, waits until
    the CLI can see the profile, and then installs. If that does not work,
    create the profile in the Profiles editor (File > Preferences > Profiles)
    and run the script again.

    Use -Profile Default for the Default profile.

.EXAMPLE
    pwsh -File install_extensions.ps1
    Installs extensions-R.txt (next to the script) into the profile "R".

.EXAMPLE
    pwsh -File install_extensions.ps1 -Profile R -List extensions-R.txt

.EXAMPLE
    pwsh -File install_extensions.ps1 -Profile R-Lecturer
    Installs extensions-R-Lecturer.txt into the profile "R-Lecturer".
#>

[CmdletBinding()]
param(
    # Name of the VS Code profile. "Profile" is an alias so that the
    # automatic variable $PROFILE is not overwritten.
    [Alias('Profile')]
    [string] $ProfileName = 'R',

    # List of extension ids. Default: extensions-<Profile>.txt next to the
    # script.
    [string] $List,

    # Seconds to wait for a newly created profile to appear.
    [int] $CreateTimeout = 60
)

$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'

# --- Find the VS Code CLI ----------------------------------------------------
$codeCmd = Get-Command code -CommandType Application -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object -First 1
if (-not $codeCmd) {
    Write-Error ("The VS Code command 'code' is not on PATH. On Windows, tick 'Add to PATH' " +
        "in the installer; on macOS, run 'Shell Command: Install code command in PATH' " +
        "from the Command Palette. Then open a new terminal.")
    exit 2
}

function Invoke-Code {
    # Runs the VS Code CLI and returns its exit code and output (stdout and
    # stderr as text), without letting stderr stop the script.
    param([string[]] $Arguments)
    $ErrorActionPreference = 'Continue'
    $PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference = $false
    $output = & $codeCmd.Source @Arguments 2>&1 | ForEach-Object { "$_" }
    [pscustomobject]@{
        ExitCode = $LASTEXITCODE
        Output   = @($output | Where-Object { $_ -ne '' })
    }
}

# --- Find the list -----------------------------------------------------------
if (-not $List) {
    $List = Join-Path $PSScriptRoot "extensions-$ProfileName.txt"
} elseif (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $List) -and -not [System.IO.Path]::IsPathRooted($List)) {
    # A relative path that is not in the current folder: try next to the script.
    $nextToScript = Join-Path $PSScriptRoot $List
    if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $nextToScript) { $List = $nextToScript }
}
if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $List -PathType Leaf)) {
    Write-Error "List not found: $List"
    exit 2
}

$ids = Get-Content -LiteralPath $List -Encoding utf8 |
    ForEach-Object { $_.Trim() } |
    Where-Object { $_ -and -not $_.StartsWith('#') } |
    Sort-Object -Unique
if (-not $ids) {
    Write-Warning "No extension ids in $List."
    exit 0
}

# --- Make sure the profile exists ---------------------------------------------
# The Default profile is used when --profile is not given.
$profileArgs = if ($ProfileName -eq 'Default') { @() } else { @('--profile', $ProfileName) }

function Get-InstalledExtensions {
    $r = Invoke-Code (@('--list-extensions') + $profileArgs)
    if ($r.ExitCode -eq 0) { return , @($r.Output) }
    if ($r.Output -match 'not found') { return $null }   # profile does not exist
    throw "code --list-extensions failed (exit $($r.ExitCode)): $($r.Output -join ' ')"
}

$installed = Get-InstalledExtensions
if ($null -eq $installed) {
    Write-Host "Profile '$ProfileName' does not exist. Opening VS Code with it once to create it..."
    $null = Invoke-Code @('--new-window', '--profile', $ProfileName)
    $deadline = (Get-Date).AddSeconds($CreateTimeout)
    while ($null -eq $installed -and (Get-Date) -lt $deadline) {
        Start-Sleep -Seconds 2
        $installed = Get-InstalledExtensions
    }
    if ($null -eq $installed) {
        Write-Error ("Profile '$ProfileName' still does not exist. Create it in VS Code " +
            "(File > Preferences > Profiles > New Profile), then run this script again.")
        exit 2
    }
    Write-Host "Profile '$ProfileName' created."
}

# --- Install -------------------------------------------------------------------
Write-Host "Profile '$ProfileName': $($ids.Count) extension(s) in $(Split-Path $List -Leaf)."
$done = [System.Collections.Generic.List[string]]::new()
$skipped = [System.Collections.Generic.List[string]]::new()
$failed = [System.Collections.Generic.List[string]]::new()

foreach ($id in $ids) {
    # Extension ids are case-insensitive; -contains compares that way too.
    if ($installed -contains $id) {
        $skipped.Add($id)
        Write-Host "  skip     $id (already installed)"
        continue
    }
    $r = Invoke-Code (@('--install-extension', $id) + $profileArgs)
    $text = $r.Output -join ' '
    if ($text -match 'built-?in') {
        # E.g. GitHub Copilot Chat, which now ships with VS Code.
        $skipped.Add($id)
        Write-Host "  skip     $id (built into VS Code)"
    } elseif ($r.ExitCode -ne 0 -or $text -match 'Failed Installing|not found') {
        $failed.Add($id)
        Write-Host "  FAILED   $id : $text" -ForegroundColor Red
    } else {
        $done.Add($id)
        Write-Host "  install  $id"
    }
}

# --- Report ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Write-Host ''
Write-Host "Installed: $($done.Count). Skipped: $($skipped.Count). Failed: $($failed.Count)."
if ($failed.Count -gt 0) {
    Write-Host 'Failed extensions:' -ForegroundColor Red
    $failed | ForEach-Object { Write-Host "  $_" -ForegroundColor Red }
    exit 1
}
exit 0

text: Collaboration is a dynamic process that involves individuals with different approaches, perspectives, and working paces. To ensure a smooth and enjoyable collaboration experience, it is important to establish clear expectations and guidelines. This collaboration guide aims to provide all the necessary information to foster effective collaboration and minimize any potential surprises along the way.

title: Collaboration Guide
text:
Lines of communication
Open and effective communication is crucial for successful collaboration. My general style of communication is “ping-pong,” meaning I prefer short exchanges frequently. Here are some preferred lines of communication:

Email
Email serves as the primary mode of communication. Feel free to reach out to me at ondrej.mottl(at)gmail.com for any queries, updates, or discussions related to our collaboration. See ways to get in touch with me.
If you expect me to respond to your email, please state it clearly.
I strive to reply to all emails as soon as possible. However, there is a chance that I may have forgotten to answer yours. If I do not respond for a significant amount of time, feel free to send me a friendly reminder. 😊⏰

Other lines of communication
In addition to email, we can also utilize collaborative platforms such as Slack, Microsoft Teams, or any other platform that suits our needs. These platforms offer faster, real-time communication, which aligns well with the “ping-pong” style of interaction.

title: Collaboration Guide
text:
GitHub
Since my primary research involves writing code, GitHub is an essential platform for any collaborative work. Check out the overview of GitHub features to get familiar with its capabilities.
I love leveraging its features, such as Issues, Pull Requests, and Projects, to streamline our collaborative coding efforts. If you are not familiar with GitHub, don’t worry! I can provide guidance and support to help you get started. It’s worth checking out their documentation for more details.
Here is my basic GitHub workflow:






flowchart
    1["Make an Issue"] --> 2("Create a new branch")
    2 --> 351471["Commit code"]
    351471 --> 257387["Create Pull Request"]
    949464{{"Does it need a review?"}} --> 625480(["Yes"])
    949464 --> 564859(["No"])
    625480 --> 752396["Assign reviewer"]
    564859 --> 715681["Squash merge PR"]
    752396 --> 715681
    257387 --> 385770["Link the Issue"]
    715681 --> 688855("Close issue (if needed)")
    688855 --> 791180["Delete the branch"]
    385770 --> 515426("Add to Project (if <span>applicable</span>)")
    515426 --> 949464
    791180 -.->|"repeat"| 2






Here are the individual steps in detail:

1. Issues
An Issue represents a single task that needs to be addressed.
Each Issue provides a platform to communicate the task with a description and the possibility to discuss details using comments. An Issue should be related to a specific problem or task. If a task is too complex or large, the Issue can be divided into several smaller ones and linked using task lists.
For more details about Issues, refer to the GitHub documentation.


2. Branches
For any code change, a new branch should be created.
Each branch should correspond to a specific task (Issue). Therefore, a branch should be named to describe the problem it is solving or directly as issue[Issue number]. If you find that the problem is too complex and needs to be split into multiple Issues or branches, you can create another branch from the current one. Branches are lightweight, so don’t worry about creating many of them.
For more details about branches, refer to the GitHub documentation.


3. Writing code
Please follow the code conventions when writing code. Commit often but make sure to keep the description for each commit meaningful.


4. Pull Request (PR)
A Pull Request is a way to merge a branch into the main branch (or another branch). The PR name should clearly indicate the purpose of the changes.
The PR details should provide an explanation of the main modifications. Additionally, you can add comments to provide further context. If possible, create the PR as a “draft” until it is ready for review and merge (learn more about drafts).
As PRs are linked to branches, and each branch should be linked to an Issue, I prefer to use the “link” functionality explicitly. This can be achieved by mentioning the Issue with specific words (e.g., close) in the PR description (see more about linking).
If you want me to review your PR before merging, simply “assign” it to me (learn more about assigning).
I prefer to merge Pull Requests using the “squash merge commit” option (learn more about it here) for a cleaner git history.


5. Projects
GitHub Projects offer a new way of project management. If we agree to use a Project in our collaboration, we will define how to collaborate individually within that project framework.

title: Collaboration Guide
text:
Manuscript writing
Writing manuscripts is a crucial aspect of scientific collaboration. The most common tools for working on a manuscript are MS Word. However, to ensure consistency and efficient collaboration during manuscript preparation, I prefer to use Google Docs, which provides real-time collaboration, and simultaneous editing, and facilitates constructive feedback on the manuscript.
In any case, I prefer to make any edits via “suggestions”. However, note that I believe that it is absolutely fine to reject suggestions (or my suggestions to be rejected).

title: Code Convention
text:
Code that follows established conventions is easier for others to read, whether they are collaborators, reviewers, or your future self several months later. Consistent code makes errors easier to find, replicated code easier to compare, and large changes possible without breaking the rest of the project.
I work mainly in the R programming language, so the rules below are R-specific. They combine the tidyverse style guide, the Google R style guide, and my own rules; where these disagree, the rules on this page win.
Style should be consistent within a project, so when you edit existing code, match the style around it.

title: Code Convention

Consistent code makes errors easier to find, replicated code easier to compare, and large changes possible without breaking the rest of the project.
I work mainly in the R programming language, so the rules below are R-specific. They combine the tidyverse style guide, the Google R style guide, and my own rules; where these disagree, the rules on this page win.

title: Code Convention
text:
R-specific
I am generally working with R programming language, so most of the specifics are related to that.

title: Code Convention
text:
Files & folders
Folders and files can have numbering to guide a user to the sequences of analyses. However, this can be added later in the project as it causes various issues with version control.

Folders names

Underscore with only the first letter capitalized (Capital_snake_style)



File naming

Underscore with only the first letter capitalized (Capital_snake_style)
File name should contain dates

dates should be in YYYY-MM-DD
see {RUtilpol} for easy handling of “version control of files”



Temporary file

temporary data files should not hold any important information
No links between Temp files and scripts on GitHub
Data/Temp should Include in .gitignore




Safe path
All paths should be using the here package to make sure that they work on all machines.

title: Code Convention
text:
Package dependencies
The {renv} package, is an R-packages dependency management, which is set up for reproducibility.
The ___Init_project___.R script is used for the preparation of all R-packages. Mainly it will install {RUtilpol} and all dependencies, which is used through the project as version control of files.

title: Code Convention
text:
Cascade of R scripts
This project is constructed using a script cascade. This means that the 00_Master.R, located within R folder, executes all scripts within sub-folders of the R folder, which in turn, executes all their sub-folders (e.g., R/01_Data_processing/Run_01.R executes R/01_Data_processing/01_full_data_process.R, R/01_Data_processing/02_data_overview.R, R/01_Data_processing/03_data_ant_counts.R, …).

title: Code Convention
text:
Configuration file
The configuration file (00_Config_file) holds the utmost importance in a project. It serves a multitude of essential purposes, such as defining global variables, loading functions, specifying file paths, and more. Every other file within a project should initiate with a reference to the configuration file (e.g., source("00_Config_file")), as it aims to minimize repetition and establish an abstraction layer that allows for centralized changes. By declaring paths in the configuration file that are utilized across multiple scripts, the user can simply refer to them by their variable name in the scripts. This approach enables seamless modifications, including renaming variables or transitioning from down-sampled to full data. All you need to do is update the relevant path in one place, and the change will automatically propagate throughout your project.

title: Code Convention
text:
One script per task
Each script should be also self-contained. It means that it should start with loading data and finish with saving results. Therefore, each script should be able to be run without having any other data in memory (except for data from 00_Config_file).
Each script should do just one task (see also file name). If it is hard to describe one task, it is better to split the script into several.

title: Code Convention
text:
Coding style
My coding style is a combination of various sources (Tidyverse, Google, and others). I am adopting it, as I am progressing in my career. However, style should be consistent at least within a single project.

title: Code Convention
text:
Code (script) structure
One script should serve one purpose and that should be obvious from its name. The script is always partitioned into clearly readable chunks (see below).

Script annotation (comments)

Script header
The script header should contain the name of the project, objectives (purpose) of that script, authors, and rough date (year of the project).
Example of a header:

#----------------------------------------------------------#
#
#
#                     Project name 
#
#                      Script name
#                      - continue
#
#                       Authors 
#                        Year
#
#----------------------------------------------------------#



Section header
Each section of a script should begin with a header which consists of a name wrapped by two lines. The name of a header should start with a capital letter. Each header name should be followed by ----- so that it is automatically picked by IDE as a section header.
Empty lines should be placed before each header to separate chunks.
Headings can have various hierarchies:

#----------------------------------------------------------#
#--------------------------------------------------#
#----------------------------------------#

Example of a header:

#----------------------------------------------------------#
# Load data -----
#----------------------------------------------------------#

Header names can be denoted by numbers, with subsections separated by *.*
Example of a numbered header:

#----------------------------------------------------------#
# 1. Estimate diversity -----
#----------------------------------------------------------#


#--------------------------------------------------#
## 1.1. Fit model -----
#--------------------------------------------------#



Single-line comments
Adding comments to code plays a pivotal role in ensuring reproducibility and preserving code knowledge for future reference. When things change or break, the user will be thankful for comments. There’s no need to comment excessively or unnecessarily, but a comment describing what a large or complex chunk of code does is always helpful. The first letter of a comment is capitalized and spaced away from the pound sign (#).
Example of a single-line comment:

# This is a comment.



Multi-line comment
Multi-line comments should start with a capital letter and the new line should start with one tab.
Example of a multi-line comment:

# This is a very long comment, where I need to describe
#    what this code is doing



Inline comment
Inline comments should always start with a space.
Example of inline comment:

function(
    agr = 1 # This is an example of an inline comment
)



Commenting functions
Function decoration should be placed before each function. See functions for details.



Code width
No line of code should be longer than 80 characters (including comments). Users can visualise the 80 characters line in selected IDER

title: Code Convention
text:
Names of objects and function

  "There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things."


Object names
Object and function should be using snake_style. The . in names is somewhat popular but it causes issues with names of methods and should be therefore avoided. The names are preferred to be very descriptive, more expressive and more explicit (note that the default linter setting of long names can be disabled).
The names should be nouns and start with the type of object:

data_* - for data

special subcategory is table_* for tables (mainly as an object for reference). Note that all tables can be data but now vice versa.

list_ - for lists
vec_ - for vectors
mod_* - for statistical model
res_ - special category, which can be used within the function to name an object to be returned (return(res_*)).

Examples of good names:

# data
data_diversity_survey

# list
list_diversity_individual_plots

# vector
vec_region_names

# model
mod_diversity_linear

# result
res_estimated_weight



Function names
Names of functions should be verbs and describe the expected functionality.
Examples of good function names

estimate_alpha_diversity()

get_first_value()

tranform_into_character()


Internal function
Note that it is possible to start a function with a "." (e.g., .get_reound_value()) flag internal functions.



Column (variable) names in data.frames
snake_style is preferred for column names in both data.frames and tibbles. Note that the janitor package can be used to edit this automatically.

title: Code Convention
text:
Syntax
Many of the syntax issues can be checked/fixed by lintr and styler packages, which can be used to automate lots of the tedious aspects.

Spaces (empty character)
Space (" ") should be always placed:

after a comma
before and after infix operators (==, +, -, <-, ~, etc.)

Exceptions:

No spaces inside or outside parentheses for regular function calls
Operators with high precedence should not be surounced by space :, ::, :::, $, @, [, [[, ^, unary -



New line (↵)
I prefer to have code more vertical than horizontal. Therefore, there are quite a lot of new lines.
Usage of a semicolon (;) to indicate a new line is not preferred.
A new line should be:

1. After an object assignment (<-)

data_diversity <-
  read_data(...)

An exception is an assignment of function.

get_data <- function(...) {
  ...
}



2. After a pipe operator (%>%)
Note that there should be a space before a pipe

data_diversity <-
  get_data() %>%
  transform_to_percentages()



3. After a function argument
This should be true for both function declaration and usage. The exception is a single argument.

get_data <- function(arg1 = foo,
                     arg2 = here::here()) {
  ...
}

data_diversity <-
  get_data(
    arg1 = foo,
    arg2 = here::here()
  )

vec_selected_regions <-
  get_regions(arg1 = foo)



4. Parentheses
Each type of parentheses (brackets) has its own rules:

round ( )

should not be placed on separate first and last line
always space before the bracket (unless it’s a function)
new line after start if it is a multi-argument function

Examples:

1 + (a + b)

get_data(arg = foo)

get_data(
  agr1 = foo,
  agr2 = here::here()
)



Square [ ]

Never space before the bracket
always space instead of missing value

Examples:

list_diversity_for_each_plot[[1]]

data_cars[, 2]



Curly { }

Use only for functions and expressions
{ should be the last character on a line and should never be on its own
} should be the first character on a line
Always new brackets after else unless followed by if
Not used for chunks of code

Examples:

get_data <- function(agr1) {
  ...
}

if (
  logical_test
) {
  ...
} else {
  ...
}

try(
  expr = {
    ...
  }
)





Assignment
Always use the left assignment <-.
Do NOT use:

right assignment (->)
equals (=)

There should be a new line after the assignment. Note that rarely singe-line assignment can be used:

data_diversity <-

Always use TRUE and FALSE, instead of T and F

title: Code Convention
text:
Functions
For function calls, always state the arguments even though R can have anonymous arguments. The only exception is for functions, where arguments are not known (i.e. ... argument).

Tidyverse
It is preferred to use the Tidyverse version of functions over base ones:



Base R
Better Style, Performance, and Utility




read.csv()
readr::read_csv()


df$some_column
df %>% dplyr::pull(some_column)


df$some_column = ...
df %>% dplyr::mutate(some_column = ...)


…
…





Namespace
Always use the full package namespace with a function call. This helps to track the source of function in a script:

data_diversity %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    beta_diverisity = 0
  )



Creating functions
Specific rules apply for making custom functions:

For naming of functions see function names
Each function (declaration) should be placed in a separate script named the function. Therefore, there should be only a single function in each function script.
function should always return (return(res_value))


Anonymous functions
In various instances, it might be better to not create a new function but to use an anonymous function (e.g. inside of purrr::map_*()).
In that case, the user should use tidle (~) for change in map default values in the function:

purrr::map(
  .f = ~ {
    mean(.x)
  }
)

For purrr::pmap_*(), the user should use ..1, ..2, etc

purrr::pmap(
  .l = list(
    list_1,
    list_2,
    list_3,
    .f = ~ {
      ..1 + ..2 + ..3
    }
  )
)



Function documentation
Each function should have documentation at the beginning of the function using the roxygen2 package. This can be useful also for project-specific functions (not just within the package) as it is easier to transition to a custom package.

title: VS Code for R
text:
The idea
One environment on every machine, with no machine-specific paths.

VS Code’s Settings Sync carries settings, keybindings, snippets, tasks and extensions between machines.
That only works if the synced files contain no user names and no install paths. So nothing in them says where R is or which version: VS Code starts radian, radian starts R, and both are found on PATH.
rig decides which R that is, per machine, with rig default. Changing the R version never touches VS Code.
The few things Sync cannot carry (task scripts, .Rprofile, PowerShell profiles) follow the same rule. .Rprofile and the PowerShell profiles are shared through OneDrive; the task scripts I copy by hand.

The key strings are ctrl+k ctrl+[Digit1] and ctrl+k ctrl+[Digit2]: scan codes, so the same physical keys on every layout.

How the presets work
VS Code has no command that sets a sidebar to a given width. It can only grow or shrink parts of the window step by step, so each preset is a long list of such steps. runCommands is built into VS Code; it runs the commands in args.commands one after the other (no extension needed).
Each sidebar ends at about its minimum width (around 170 px) plus N steps of about 60 px. Zoom and display scaling change the pixel values.
Two facts drive the sequence:

workbench.action.increaseViewWidth and workbench.action.decreaseViewWidth always resize the editor area. The space comes from, or goes to, the primary sidebar first, then the secondary sidebar.
workbench.action.increaseViewSize and workbench.action.decreaseViewSize resize the focused part. But VS Code does not notice focus inside a webview (such as a chat view in the secondary sidebar), so these cannot size the secondary sidebar directly.

So the secondary sidebar is sized indirectly. Preset 1, step by step:

workbench.action.closeSidebar: hide the primary sidebar. Hidden, it absorbs nothing.
workbench.action.increaseViewWidth, 20 times: grow the editor area. The space comes from the secondary sidebar until it is at its minimum.
workbench.action.decreaseViewWidth, 4 times: shrink the editor 4 steps. The secondary sidebar gets them: minimum plus 4 steps.
workbench.action.focusSideBar: reopen and focus the primary sidebar. It takes its space from the editor.
workbench.action.decreaseViewSize, 20 times: shrink the focused primary sidebar to its minimum.
workbench.action.increaseViewSize, 2 times: grow it 2 steps.
workbench.action.focusActiveEditorGroup: put the cursor back in the editor.

The 20s only push a part to its limit; extra steps at the limit do nothing. If a sidebar does not reach its minimum on a very wide screen, add more of those lines.

text:
Settings Sync
Settings Sync keeps profiles, settings, keybindings, snippets, tasks, extensions and UI state the same on every machine where you sign in. Change a setting once, on any machine, and it travels. That only works if the synced files contain no machine-specific paths (How the pieces fit).

The gotcha: some settings never sync
Sync silently skips three kinds of settings:

those marked machine (they only make sense on one computer),
those marked machine-overridable,
those flagged never to sync by their extension.

vscode-R marks several of its settings like that: r.consolePath, r.executablePath, r.consoleArgs, r.consoleSendDelay and r.plot.backend.
The fix is the settingsSync.ignoredSettings list. A leading - means “include this after all”:
"settingsSync.ignoredSettings": ["-r.consolePath", "-r.plot.backend"]

It must be in the Default profile, where VS Code reads application-scoped settings. I keep the same line in each synced profile as well.
To see what was uploaded: Settings Sync: Show Synced Data.

The two settings it opts back in are safe to sync because they hold no paths: r.consolePath is just "radian" (found on PATH), and r.plot.backend is "httpgd".

Settings reference
text:
This page goes through the settings.json of my R profile, the one profile I use for all R work. It is synced between my machines with Settings Sync. Profiles do not inherit settings from the Default profile, so copying this file into a new profile gives the same set-up. The exceptions are a few application-wide settings, which VS Code always reads from the Default profile (see settingsSync.ignoredSettings below). Settings Sync and the two R settings
Settings Sync skips settings that are scoped machine or machine-overridable, or marked ignoreSync. Two settings this set-up depends on are affected: r.consolePath is machine-overridable, and r.plot.backend is ignoreSync. Without the line below, a new machine would get the rest of the profile but not radian and not httpgd.
settingsSync.ignoredSettings is the list of settings Sync should skip. A leading - does the opposite: it opts a setting back in. So ["-r.consolePath", "-r.plot.backend"] makes Sync carry both.
settingsSync.ignoredSettings itself is an application-scoped setting: VS Code reads it from the Default profile only. The same line therefore also has to be in the Default profile’s settings.json, otherwise it has no effect. See Profiles and Settings Sync.


Plots: httpgd
With r.plot.backend: "httpgd", plots open in a VS Code tab that resizes the plot with the window and keeps a plot history. It needs the httpgd R package in every R version I use; with rig, each version has its own library, so I install it per version (R versions with rig).

With github.copilot.editor.enableAutoCompletions: false and github.copilot.nextEditSuggestions.enabled: true, Copilot does not complete code as I type. The Generate Commit Message button in Source Control reads .github/commit-instructions.md from the root of the open repository and follows it. The path is relative, so each repository can have its own rules; if the file does not exist, Copilot uses its default style. My Project_template ships this file, so every project made from it has the same commit conventions.

multiCommand.commands belongs to the multi-command extension (ryuta46.multi-command). Each entry defines a new command (command) that runs a list of existing commands (sequence) one after the other.









Setting
Value
What it does
Why




multiCommand.commands
7 entries, see below
Defines commands that run a sequence of other commands.
Chunk navigation and “run chunk and move” in R Markdown and Quarto.



"multiCommand.commands": [
  { "command": "multiCommand.r.go.previous.chunk.center", "sequence": ["r.goToPreviousChunk"] },
  { "command": "multiCommand.r.go.next.chunk.center",     "sequence": ["r.goToNextChunk"] },
  { "command": "multicmd.r.go.beginning.chunk.center",    "sequence": ["r.selectCurrentChunk", "cursorLeft", "cursorDown"] },
  { "command": "multicmd.r.go.end.chunk.center",          "sequence": ["r.selectCurrentChunk", "cursorRight", "cursorLineStart", "cursorUp"] },
  { "command": "multicmd.r.run.previous.chunk.center",    "sequence": ["r.goToPreviousChunk", "r.runCurrentChunk"] },
  { "command": "multicmd.r.run.chunk.move.end",           "sequence": ["r.runCurrentChunk", "multicmd.r.go.end.chunk.center"] },
  { "command": "multicmd.r.run.next.chunk.move.end",      "sequence": ["r.goToNextChunk", "multicmd.r.go.end.chunk.center", "r.runCurrentChunk"] }
]
(Shortened to one line per entry; the full file has the same content spread over more lines.) What each one does, in plain words. The r.* commands come from vscode-R and work on the code chunks of R Markdown and Quarto documents.







Command
What it does




multiCommand.r.go.previous.chunk.center
Go to the previous chunk.


multiCommand.r.go.next.chunk.center
Go to the next chunk.


multicmd.r.go.beginning.chunk.center
Jump to the start of the current chunk: select the chunk, collapse the selection to its first line, then move one line down onto the code.


multicmd.r.go.end.chunk.center
Jump to the end of the current chunk: select the chunk, collapse the selection to its end, go to the start of that line (the closing fence), then one line up onto the last line of code.


multicmd.r.run.previous.chunk.center
Go to the previous chunk and run it.


multicmd.r.run.chunk.move.end
Run the current chunk, then jump to its last line.


multicmd.r.run.next.chunk.move.end
Go to the next chunk, jump to its last line, and run it.



Points to know:

Wrappers. The two multiCommand.r.go.*.chunk.center entries each run a single command, so they do exactly what r.goToPreviousChunk and r.goToNextChunk do on their own.
Nesting. Two sequences call multicmd.r.go.end.chunk.center, so one multi-command can be a step in another.
“center”. Despite the names, no sequence scrolls or centres the view; they only move the cursor and run code.
Not bound to keys. No keybinding in this profile’s keybindings.json uses these commands. They are available through Command Palette → Multi command: Execute multi command, or for a keybinding of your own, for example:

{
  "key": "<your key>",
  "command": "extension.multiCommand.execute",
  "args": { "command": "multicmd.r.run.next.chunk.move.end" },
  "when": "editorTextFocus"
}
VS Code also has a built-in runCommands command that runs a list of commands from a keybinding without any extension; the layout presets on Keybindings use it.

text:
radian or VS Code starts an old R version
radian --version or R.version.string shows an older R than your rig default version.
Cause: something pins R before rig gets a say:

an R_HOME environment variable. It can be a user variable as well as a system one;
a version folder such as C:\Program Files\R\R-x.y.z\bin on PATH;
a workspace .vscode/settings.json with r.executablePath or --r-binary (that one is on purpose, see R versions).

Group Description
Welcome to the Laboratory of Quantitative Ecology, where we are dedicated to unraveling the complexities of vegetation dynamics. Our research spans spatio-temporal scales, investigating both historical and contemporary factors that shape ecological patterns of ecosystems.

Research Focus
Delving into various facets of biodiversity, including taxonomic, functional, and phylogenetic dimensions, we utilize advanced quantitative palaeoecological methods, data science, and machine learning. Our investigations cover diverse spatial scales, from local biomes to continents, enriched by the inclusion of long-term data, such as fossil pollen records and other ecological archives.

State-of-the-Art Tools and Methods
We use cutting-edge quantitative and statistical methods, alongside state-of-the-art data science and machine learning approaches. Our research not only involves the application of existing methods but also the development of new methodologies to extract deeper insights from complex ecological datasets. This continuous innovation ensures that our research remains at the forefront of ecological science, expanding the limits of our understanding of vegetation patterns.


Interdisciplinary Approach
Our research integrates concepts and methodologies from various fields, including macroecology, palaeoecology, biodiversity science, and quantitative ecology. This interdisciplinary perspective allows us to gain a comprehensive understanding of vegetation dynamics and their underlying drivers.

title: Open Palaeoecological Data
text:
Project website
  
  
    
     COST Action record
  

  
  
Open Palaeoecological Data (PalaeOpen) - analysing the past, building foresight is an Action funded by European Cooperation in Science and Technology - COST.


Restoring and managing nature during times of rapid environmental change requires knowledge of ecosystem response to climate and land use change on timescales of decades to millennia. Different palaeoecological disciplines have collected relevant, site-specific data during the last decades. Much of the palaeoecological data are currently dispersed across different repositories, databases and largely not publicly available.
This Action aims to meet the challenge of bringing much of these data into the public domain, harmonise their taxonomy and metadata, and make them relevant to nature conservation. By combining domain specific repositories and databases, the Action will unlock these data collections and make them available for palaeoecological meta-analysis of ecosystem interactions on a continental scale. This will permit integrated analysis of terrestrial and aquatic ecosystem responses to natural and anthropogenic environmental change for the first time. The Action will overcome the barriers between palaeoecologist, macroecologists and nature conservation practitioners by developing and engaging with a new research agenda.
Scientific workshops in different parts of Europe will provide formats to interact with local nature conservation practitioners. The research agenda will address the knowledge gaps in nature conservation as well as the need to understand continental scale interactions of ecosystem components, including lagged or threshold responses. A dedicated outreach working group will ensure that the new knowledge is also accessible to the public. Moreover, the group will develop educational material for schools and universities based on the collected data.
For project news and further information, visit the PalaeOpen website. The COST Action record provides the formal Action details.



I serve on the Steering Committee and co-lead Working Group 3, “Data Storage and Management”. I contribute expertise in palaeoecological data processing and help develop and coordinate the Action.
The logo shown above is the official project logo from the PalaeOpen website.

{RRatepol} is an R package for estimating rate of change (RoC) from community data in time series.
{RRatepol} is written as an R package and includes a range of possible settings including a novel method to evaluate RoC in a single stratigraphical sequence using assemblage data and age uncertainties for each level. There are multiple built-in dissimilarity coefficients (dissimilarity_coefficient) for different types of assemblage data, and various levels of data smoothing that can be applied depending on the type and variance of the data. In addition, {RRatepol} can use randomisation, accompanied by use of age uncertainties of each level and taxon standardisation to detect RoC patterns in datasets with high data noise or variability (i.e. numerous rapid changes in composition or sedimentation rates).

My set-up in short
I use VS Code with the vscode-R extension for all my R work, on Windows. R runs in radian, a modern R console with syntax highlighting and multi-line editing, opened in a terminal panel docked on the right. Plots go to the httpgd viewer inside VS Code. The languageserver package gives autocompletion, hover help and go to definition; lintr checks the code as I type, and styler formats it when I ask. I write documents, slides and this website in Quarto, with the Quarto extension for preview and code-chunk execution. rig manages several R versions side by side, and renv with targets keeps each project reproducible (project template). Git work happens in the built-in Source Control view, with GitLens, Git Graph and the GitHub Pull Requests extension. For AI help I use GitHub Copilot and Claude Code. The look is the built-in Visual Studio Dark theme with vscode-icons, and a set of custom keybindings (for example Ctrl+Shift+M for the pipe) makes the common R actions one keystroke. Everything is kept in one VS Code profile called R, synced between my machines.
It pairs with two other things I use daily:

my project template for reproducible R projects (renv, targets, tests, instructions for coding assistants);
the R Version Switcher extension, for per-project R versions (R versions).
